title: Ethnopharmacological Review of Medicinal Plants Used in the Management of Diabetes in Morocco

subsections.section_title: Diabetes Burden and the Ethnopharmacological Context in Morocco
subsections.content:
Diabetes has become a major non-communicable disease challenge in Morocco, reflecting the country’s rapid demographic, nutritional, and lifestyle transition. National and regional analyses indicate that type 2 diabetes predominates and is increasing in parallel with urbanization, population ageing, obesity, and reduced physical activity, placing Morocco within the broader North African belt of high metabolic risk ref [1], ref [2]. Comparative estimates from international surveillance frameworks have likewise classified Morocco among the countries with a substantial and growing adult diabetes burden, with many cases remaining undiagnosed until complications emerge ref [3], ref [4].

Population-based Moroccan studies also show that diabetes clusters with other cardiometabolic risk factors. Surveys in Moroccan adults have documented high frequencies of overweight/obesity, hypertension, and impaired glucose regulation, especially among women and urban residents, underscoring the syndemic nature of chronic disease risk ref [5], ref [6]. This epidemiological profile is particularly important because late diagnosis and suboptimal long-term control contribute to microvascular and macrovascular complications, amplifying pressure on health services and household finances.

The burden is not evenly distributed. Social inequalities, differences between urban and rural settings, and varying access to screening and continuity of care shape detection and outcomes. In Moroccan primary care cohorts, glycaemic control has often been inadequate, suggesting that prevalence figures alone underestimate the true clinical and economic impact of the disease ref [7], ref [8]. These epidemiological realities help explain why diabetes management in Morocco extends beyond biomedical services and intersects with traditional therapeutic practices.

subsections.section_title: Diabetes Burden and the Ethnopharmacological Context in Morocco
subsections.subsection_title: Healthcare access and reliance on traditional medicine
subsections.content:
Access to diabetes care in Morocco is shaped by marked territorial and socioeconomic inequalities. National analyses of health financing and service delivery have shown persistent out-of-pocket expenditure, uneven distribution of healthcare infrastructure, and weaker continuity of care in rural and peri-urban settings, all of which can delay diagnosis and compromise long-term management of chronic diseases such as diabetes ref [9], ref [10]. These structural constraints are compounded by the need for repeated monitoring, dietary counseling, and sustained pharmacotherapy, making diabetes particularly sensitive to gaps in accessibility and affordability.

Within this context, traditional medicine remains an important therapeutic recourse. Ethnobotanical surveys from different Moroccan regions repeatedly report the use of medicinal plants for metabolic disorders, including remedies specifically identified for diabetes or symptoms associated with hyperglycemia ref [11], ref [12], ref [13]. Such practices are not simply substitutes for biomedical care; they are embedded in household knowledge, local markets, and longstanding healer traditions, and they may be used before consultation, alongside prescribed drugs, or when formal care is perceived as financially or geographically difficult to access ref [11], ref [14].

This reliance has two implications for diabetes research and policy. First, it underscores the need to document actual community practices rather than assuming exclusive dependence on biomedical treatment. Second, it raises questions of safety, efficacy, dosage standardization, and herb-drug interactions, especially because antidiabetic plant use is common in North African and Middle Eastern settings more broadly ref [14], ref [15]. Recognizing this interface between constrained healthcare access and plural therapeutic behavior is therefore essential for an ethnopharmacological survey focused on Morocco.

subsections.section_title: Diabetes Burden and the Ethnopharmacological Context in Morocco
subsections.content:
Ethnopharmacology is an interdisciplinary field that investigates biologically active substances used in traditional medical systems, linking local therapeutic knowledge with pharmacognosy, phytochemistry, pharmacology, toxicology, and clinical evaluation. Its modern scope extends beyond simple plant listing: it asks how remedies are selected, prepared, transmitted, and validated within specific cultural settings, while also examining efficacy and safety through experimental methods ref [16], ref [17]. In this sense, ethnopharmacology is especially relevant to diabetes, a chronic disorder for which long-term self-care, symptom interpretation, and culturally familiar remedies often shape treatment behavior.

Methodologically, ethnopharmacological research moves from emic knowledge to laboratory and, ideally, clinical assessment. Quantitative ethnobotanical tools help identify culturally salient species, while bioassay-guided approaches, metabolomics, and mechanism-oriented studies can clarify antidiabetic actions such as modulation of carbohydrate digestion, insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, oxidative stress, and inflammation ref [18], ref [19]. At the same time, the field increasingly emphasizes evidence hierarchies, rigorous botanical identification, reproducible extraction protocols, and critical appraisal of toxicity and herb–drug interactions, particularly for chronic diseases requiring prolonged use ref [17], ref [20].

For Morocco, the scope of ethnopharmacology is therefore not limited to documenting vernacular remedies; it also includes conservation of biocultural heritage, assessment of regional materia medica, and translation of traditional practices into evidence-based complementary care. Mediterranean and North African traditions offer rich therapeutic repertoires, but their medical relevance depends on integrating ethnographic context with pharmacological validation and ethical frameworks for knowledge use and benefit sharing ref [21], ref [22]. This integrated perspective justifies a focused survey of Moroccan antidiabetic plants.

subsections.section_title: Diabetes Burden and the Ethnopharmacological Context in Morocco
subsections.subsection_title: Historical foundations of Moroccan herbal medicine
subsections.content:
Moroccan herbal medicine is historically rooted in a layered medical culture shaped by Amazigh, Arab-Islamic, Andalusian, sub-Saharan, and Mediterranean exchanges. Classical Greco-Arab medicine, transmitted through Islamic scholarship, provided an enduring theoretical framework in which diet, simples, and compound remedies were used to restore humoral balance, while local pharmacopoeias incorporated regionally available plants and empirically valued preparations ref [23], ref [24]. This synthesis helped produce a durable household and market-based tradition in which plants remained central to everyday therapeutics.

The historical continuity of this tradition is visible in Morocco’s medicinal plant markets, vernacular materia medica, and the persistence of specialist herbalists. Ethnobotanical studies from different Moroccan regions repeatedly show that current uses are embedded in inherited knowledge systems rather than being merely opportunistic responses to modern healthcare gaps ref [25], ref [26]. Surveys of traditional pharmacopoeia in eastern Morocco and other areas document a broad repertoire of medicinal species and preparation methods, indicating a long-standing process of selection, adaptation, and transmission across generations ref [27], ref [28].

These historical foundations are especially relevant for antidiabetic ethnopharmacology. The prominence of food-medicines, bitter herbs, aromatic seeds, and polyherbal remedies in Moroccan practice reflects older therapeutic logics that linked chronic metabolic disturbances to digestion, lifestyle, and bodily balance ref [24], ref [29]. Contemporary reviews of Moroccan medicinal flora further suggest that this inherited knowledge base remains a major reservoir for selecting candidate antidiabetic plants for pharmacological investigation ref [28], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Diabetes Burden and the Ethnopharmacological Context in Morocco
subsections.subsection_title: Rationale for a focused survey on antidiabetic plants
subsections.content:
A focused survey on antidiabetic plants in Morocco is justified by the convergence of three factors: the growing burden of diabetes, the continued recourse to medicinal plants in everyday care, and the exceptional botanical and cultural diversity of the country. Morocco is recognized as a Mediterranean biodiversity hotspot, with marked floristic richness and a long history of Arabic, Amazigh, Andalusian, and sub-Saharan therapeutic traditions, creating a particularly dense reservoir of plant knowledge that may contain both widely shared and locally specific antidiabetic remedies ref [31], ref [32].

From a research perspective, ethnobotanical documentation of Moroccan medicinal flora is substantial but fragmented across regions, indications, and methodological approaches. Reviews of Moroccan aromatic and medicinal plants and regional ethnobotanical surveys repeatedly note species used against symptoms consistent with diabetes, yet these data are dispersed and often not synthesized around antidiabetic use specifically ref [33], ref [27], ref [34]. A dedicated survey therefore helps consolidate vernacular knowledge, identify recurrent taxa, and distinguish highly cited species from anecdotal reports.

Such synthesis is also pharmacologically relevant. International assessments have emphasized that traditional antidiabetic plants remain important leads for bioactive compound discovery, while evidence quality varies widely across species and study designs ref [35], ref [36]. In Morocco, where herbal medicines are commonly commercialized through informal and semi-formal channels, a focused review can additionally support prioritization for phytochemical, toxicological, and clinical evaluation, especially because medicinal plants may carry risks related to misidentification, adulteration, or inappropriate dosing ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Ethnobotanical Diversity of Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
Ethnobotanical surveys conducted in different Moroccan regions indicate that the inventory of plants used traditionally against diabetes is broad and taxonomically heterogeneous, often comprising several dozen species within a single province and well over one hundred species when datasets are pooled nationally. Recurrent reports from High Atlas, Rif, Oriental, and pre-Saharan communities show that certain species repeatedly appear in antidiabetic repertoires, notably Trigonella foenum-graecum, Olea europaea, Artemisia herba-alba, Ajuga iva, Allium cepa, Allium sativum, Salvia officinalis, and Marrubium vulgare, alongside numerous locally specific taxa recorded in regional studies ref [38], ref [27], ref [39].

This inventory is not merely a species list but a reflection of plural therapeutic traditions. Surveys from Errachidia, Tafilalet, Fez-Boulemane, and other Moroccan settings document overlap between food plants, aromatic herbs, and strongly bioactive wild medicinal species, with leaves, seeds, and aerial parts most often cited for decoctions or infusions ref [27], ref [40], ref [41]. Such inventories also show that antidiabetic use is embedded in wider polyherbal and multipurpose practice: the same plants may be prescribed for hypertension, digestive disorders, or renal complications associated with diabetes ref [39], ref [28].

Taken together, the reported inventories suggest a dynamic pharmacopoeia shaped by ecology, market availability, and intergenerational knowledge. Reviews synthesizing Moroccan medicinal flora consistently identify antidiabetic plants as one of the richest use categories, while emphasizing that frequency of citation varies by region and does not necessarily imply pharmacological equivalence or safety ref [28], ref [42], ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Ethnobotanical Diversity of Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
Across Moroccan ethnobotanical surveys of diabetes, antidiabetic remedies are distributed across many angiosperm lineages, but a limited number of families recur with high frequency. Lamiaceae, Asteraceae, Fabaceae, Apiaceae, and Oleaceae are repeatedly prominent, reflecting both the floristic richness of Mediterranean Morocco and the strong place of aromatic, food-medicinal, and shrubby taxa in domestic therapeutics ref [44], ref [45], ref [46]. This pattern is consistent with broader North African and Mediterranean ethnopharmacological inventories, where these families contribute a large share of species used for metabolic disorders ref [47].

Within these families, several taxa appear especially dominant in Moroccan reports. Trigonella foenum-graecum, Olea europaea, Artemisia herba-alba, Rosmarinus officinalis (now Salvia rosmarinus), Lavandula species, Ajuga iva, and Nigella sativa are among the most recurrently cited plants, alongside widely used food plants such as Allium cepa and Allium sativum ref [44], ref [45], ref [48]. Their prominence likely reflects a combination of ecological availability, incorporation into everyday diet, and a reputation for glycemic control reinforced by experimental literature on hypoglycemic or antihyperglycemic activity ref [49], ref [50].

At a taxonomic level, the dominance of Lamiaceae and Asteraceae is noteworthy because these families are rich in essential-oil and phenolic-producing species, traits often associated in local pharmacopoeias with “purifying,” digestive, and metabolic effects. Fabaceae and Apiaceae contribute both seeds and aerial parts, while Oleaceae is represented above all by the olive tree, a culturally central species in Morocco ref [46], ref [48], ref [51]. Thus, family-level dominance is not merely botanical: it reflects the intersection of regional biodiversity, culinary-medical overlap, and long-standing therapeutic preference.

subsections.section_title: Ethnobotanical Diversity of Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
The regional distribution of antidiabetic medicinal plants in Morocco broadly follows the country’s major bioclimatic and phytogeographic gradients. Ethnobotanical surveys repeatedly show high reporting frequencies in the Rif, Middle Atlas, High Atlas, Anti-Atlas, and pre-Saharan zones, where floristic richness intersects with strong reliance on household phytotherapy. Studies from eastern Morocco and the central Middle Atlas indicate that mountain and piedmont environments supply a large share of species gathered for diabetes management, including aromatic shrubs, perennial herbs, and woody taxa adapted to Mediterranean and montane climates [1,2].

Ecological distribution is equally important: many frequently cited antidiabetic taxa are associated with semi-arid scrublands, maquis, forest clearings, and steppe-like habitats, while others are obtained from oasis agroecosystems or cultivated fields. Surveys in the High Atlas and Tafilalet–Draa regions emphasize the importance of arid and Saharan ecotones, where local pharmacopoeias integrate wild desert species with irrigated garden plants [3,4]. In contrast, humid and subhumid northern areas contribute taxa from forested and littoral environments, reflecting Morocco’s marked ecological heterogeneity [5].

This regional pattern also implies uneven harvesting pressure. Wild-collected species remain prominent in mountain, forest, and rangeland settings, whereas cultivated medicinal-food plants are more common in peri-urban plains and oasis systems. Comparative ethnobotanical work from the Rif and eastern Morocco suggests that accessibility, altitude, rainfall regime, and market integration all shape which antidiabetic plants are known, traded, and therapeutically preferred across communities [1,5,6].

subsections.section_title: Ethnobotanical Diversity of Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
Vernacular nomenclature is central to how antidiabetic plants are recognized, classified, and transmitted in Moroccan ethnobotany. Across Arabic- and Amazigh-speaking settings, plant names often encode morphology, taste, habitat, or perceived therapeutic action, allowing communities to distinguish useful taxa without recourse to formal botanical terminology. Ethnobotanical surveys from different Moroccan regions show that the same species may circulate under multiple local names, while one vernacular label may also refer to more than one botanical taxon, creating challenges for pharmacological standardization and for comparing inventories across studies ref [1], ref [2].

This linguistic variability is especially important for widely used antidiabetic plants such as fenugreek, olive, wormwood, and pennyroyal, whose local identification is embedded in culinary, pastoral, and domestic practice rather than in a narrowly medical sphere. Regional studies in eastern Morocco, the Rif, and the High Atlas indicate that accurate cultural identification usually depends on a combination of name, plant part, collection site, and preparation method, with women herbal users, traditional healers, and rural elders acting as key validators of authenticity ref [3], ref [4], ref [5]. Such contextual identification helps prevent substitution, but it is also vulnerable to market-mediated simplification, where traders may collapse several taxa under a commercially dominant name ref [6].

For survey research, vernacular data therefore have dual value: they document cultural knowledge systems and provide clues to emic disease concepts, but they must be cross-checked with voucher specimens and taxonomic revision. Moroccan ethnobotanical methodology increasingly emphasizes this linkage because local names alone can obscure cryptic diversity, especially in species-rich genera and in multispecies herbal mixtures used for diabetes management ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Ethnobotanical Diversity of Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
In Moroccan antidiabetic ethnobotany, wild-harvested species generally outnumber cultivated ones, reflecting the continuing importance of surrounding forests, scrublands, steppe margins, and mountain habitats as sources of medicinal raw material. Broad ethnobotanical syntheses from Morocco repeatedly show that many frequently cited taxa are collected from natural vegetation, whereas cultivated plants are often drawn from home gardens, orchards, or local markets, especially when they also serve culinary functions ref [57], ref [58]. This wild bias is partly explained by the floristic richness of Mediterranean and montane environments and by the persistence of gathering knowledge among rural communities ref [59], ref [60].

Cultivated antidiabetic plants nevertheless occupy a significant complementary niche. Species such as olive, fenugreek, garlic, onion, and certain aromatic herbs are readily accessible, storable, and embedded in food-medicine continuums, which facilitates repeated use in chronic conditions such as diabetes ref [58], ref [61]. Market integration also blurs the wild/cultivated distinction, because many remedies are purchased from herbalists without clear information on provenance; traded materia medica may include both locally gathered wild taxa and cultivated or imported products ref [62].

From a conservation perspective, reliance on wild populations raises concerns when roots, bark, or whole plants are harvested, particularly in arid and montane zones where regeneration is slow. Moroccan and North African studies on medicinal plant trade and use have therefore emphasized the need to promote cultivation of high-demand species, standardize sourcing, and document ecological status alongside therapeutic reputation ref [60], ref [62], ref [63]. In this sense, the wild-versus-cultivated axis is not merely descriptive: it shapes accessibility, seasonal availability, quality control, and the sustainability of antidiabetic plant use in Morocco.

subsections.section_title: Ethnobotanical Diversity of Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
Ethnobotanical studies from Morocco consistently show that knowledge of antidiabetic plants is unevenly distributed across communities and is often concentrated among older adults, herbalists, traditional healers, and women responsible for household healthcare. Surveys in different Moroccan regions report that practical expertise on plant identification, dosage, and preparation is commonly held by elderly informants and market-based herb sellers, while younger generations tend to possess more fragmented knowledge, suggesting an age-related erosion of transmission continuity ref [64], ref [65], ref [66]. This pattern aligns with broader North African and Mediterranean observations that specialist and domestic domains of medicinal knowledge coexist rather than being fully separate ref [67].

Transmission pathways are predominantly oral and experiential. Within families, recipes for decoctions, infusions, and mixtures used for diabetes are typically passed from parents or grandparents to children through repeated participation in collection and preparation, whereas outside the household, knowledge circulates through neighborhood advice networks, rural gathering practices, and commercial interactions in souks and herb shops ref [65], ref [66], ref [68]. Moroccan ethnobotanical records also indicate that vernacular classifications and therapeutic indications are reinforced through local social memory, with recurrent consultation of respected healers or herbal vendors when chronic conditions such as diabetes require long-term management ref [64], ref [69].

At the same time, transmission is no longer exclusively oral. Several Moroccan studies note the growing influence of literacy, mass media, and semi-formal phytotherapy publications, which can expand access but also standardize or decontextualize locally specific practices ref [68], ref [70]. This hybridization of knowledge systems is important for antidiabetic plant use: it may facilitate wider circulation of reputed species, yet it can also weaken safeguards traditionally provided by experienced knowledge holders regarding toxicity, contraindications, and preparation-specific efficacy ref [67], ref [71].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Therapeutic Practices and Modes of Use
subsections.subsection_title: Plant parts utilized in diabetes remedies
subsections.content:
Ethnobotanical studies of antidiabetic practice in Morocco indicate a marked preference for aerial organs, especially leaves, followed by seeds, fruits, and, less frequently, roots, bark, bulbs, or the whole plant. This pattern is consistent with broader North African and Mediterranean herbal repertoires, where leaves are favored because they are readily collected, easily dried, and commonly used in infusions or decoctions, while seeds and fruits are often linked to spice-medicines such as fenugreek or cumin that circulate between domestic food and therapy ref [72], ref [73], ref [74].

The choice of plant part is not only practical but also pharmacological. Leaves and flowering tops are often selected in taxa rich in phenolics and volatile constituents, whereas seeds are preferred in species valued for mucilage, fixed oils, or characteristic secondary metabolites associated with glycemic regulation. Reviews of Moroccan antidiabetic flora repeatedly note frequent use of leaves of Olea europaea and Trigonella foenum-graecum seeds, alongside fruits or cladodes of species such as Opuntia ficus-indica, illustrating how part selection follows local perceptions of where the plant’s “active strength” resides ref [75], ref [76], ref [56].

At the same time, reliance on roots, bulbs, latex-bearing tissues, or bark is generally more limited, partly because these parts may be harder to process, seasonally constrained, or more strongly associated with safety concerns and ecological pressure from destructive harvesting. This has implications for sustainability: harvesting leaves, fruits, or seeds is usually less damaging than uprooting entire plants, an issue highlighted in ethnopharmacological assessments of medicinal plants used for diabetes and related chronic disorders in Morocco ref [73], ref [77], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Therapeutic Practices and Modes of Use
subsections.content:
In Moroccan ethnomedical practice, antidiabetic plants are most commonly prepared as simple water-based formulations, especially decoctions and infusions made from leaves, seeds, bark, or aerial parts. Surveys from different Moroccan regions consistently report that decoction is favored when tougher materials are used and when a stronger extract is culturally considered desirable, whereas infusion is more often associated with aromatic or delicate taxa; powders, macerates, and fresh juice are reported less frequently but remain part of household therapeutics ref [44], ref [78], ref [79]. This predominance of aqueous preparations reflects both domestic practicality and continuity with broader Mediterranean and Maghrebi herbal traditions.

Dosage forms are usually non-industrial and measured through vernacular units such as cups, glasses, pinches, or spoonfuls rather than standardized weights. Plant material may be taken alone or mixed with honey, milk, olive oil, or common foods to improve palatability and regularity of use, blurring the boundary between remedy and diet. Ethnobotanical studies from eastern Morocco, the High Atlas, and neighboring North African settings show that these preparations are generally consumed daily or several times per day over prolonged periods, often alongside dietary restriction and other self-care measures ref [78], ref [80], ref [81], ref [82].

Preparation choices also encode therapeutic reasoning. Bitter decoctions are often regarded as more potent for lowering blood sugar, while powdered seeds or leaves are valued for convenient repeated administration and for incorporation into food. Reviews of Moroccan medicinal plants used in diabetes further note that aqueous household preparations dominate despite the fact that experimentally active fractions are sometimes obtained with organic solvents, underscoring a gap between traditional dosage forms and pharmacological standardization ref [83], ref [84].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Therapeutic Practices and Modes of Use
subsections.subsection_title: Routes of administration and treatment regimens
subsections.content:
Across Moroccan ethnobotanical reports on diabetes, the dominant route of administration is oral, most commonly as decoctions, infusions, macerates, or powdered plant material taken with water, milk, honey, or food. Surveys from different Moroccan regions consistently describe remedies being consumed once to three times daily, usually over prolonged periods and often without rigid standardization of dose, reflecting household measures such as a glass, spoonful, pinch, or handful rather than fixed pharmaceutical units ref [72], ref [85], ref [86]. This oral emphasis is coherent with local understandings of diabetes as a chronic internal imbalance requiring repeated regulation rather than short-course intervention.

Treatment regimens are commonly individualized and adaptive. Patients may begin with a single plant and then shift to mixtures when glycemic control is perceived as inadequate, while dose intensity can be reduced after symptomatic improvement. Ethnopharmacological studies from Moroccan communities note that administration is frequently timed around meals or fasting periods and may be continued alongside biomedical antidiabetic drugs, creating a pragmatic pluralism in care seeking ref [85], ref [87], ref [88]. Such patterns raise important questions about cumulative exposure, adherence, and herb-drug interactions, especially for plants repeatedly highlighted as highly cited antidiabetic remedies in Morocco ref [89], ref [90].

External routes appear much less central for diabetes itself, though topical applications may be used for associated wounds or skin problems rather than for glycemic regulation. Overall, the regimen logic is therefore chronic, oral, and experience-based, with treatment success judged by changes in thirst, urination, fatigue, appetite, or body weight as much as by formal glucose measurement ref [72], ref [86], ref [91].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Therapeutic Practices and Modes of Use
subsections.content:
Polyherbalism is a recurrent feature of Moroccan antidiabetic practice, where remedies are often built from two or more species rather than from a single plant. Ethnobotanical surveys from different Moroccan regions report mixtures combining aromatic, bitter, and mucilaginous taxa, with frequent inclusion of species such as Trigonella foenum-graecum, Artemisia herba-alba, Origanum compactum, Nigella sativa, and Olea europaea leaves in household diabetes recipes or broader metabolic formulations ref [64], ref [92], ref [93]. Such combinations are usually justified locally through notions of strengthening efficacy, reducing adverse effects, and addressing the complex symptom cluster associated with diabetes, including thirst, polyuria, fatigue, and digestive disturbance.

This combinatorial logic is consistent with wider herbal medicine frameworks in which multi-component preparations are used to target several physiological processes simultaneously, including delayed carbohydrate absorption, improved insulin sensitivity, antioxidant protection, and moderation of chronic inflammation ref [94], ref [95]. Experimental literature also supports the plausibility of synergy among phytochemical classes commonly co-present in Moroccan mixtures—polyphenols, terpenoids, sulfur compounds, and soluble fibers—even though most studies evaluate isolated plants rather than exact traditional recipes ref [94], ref [96]. Consequently, the rationale for plant combinations is pharmacologically credible but remains under-validated for the precise formulations used in community practice.

A further feature of Moroccan polyherbal use is overlap between medicine and diet: seeds, leaves, and culinary spices are frequently combined as decoctions, powders, or infused blends taken daily over long periods. This resembles broader Mediterranean and North African traditions in which antidiabetic care is embedded in routine food practices rather than confined to discrete medicinal products ref [92], ref [97]. However, the variability of ingredients, proportions, and treatment duration complicates standardization and safety assessment, particularly when combinations are self-prescribed or used alongside biomedical therapy ref [93], ref [98].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Therapeutic Practices and Modes of Use
subsections.subsection_title: Use in relation to symptoms and complications
subsections.content:
In Moroccan ethnomedical practice, antidiabetic plants are often selected not only for reducing glycaemia but also for addressing the symptom clusters through which diabetes is locally recognized, including excessive thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, weight loss, and delayed wound healing. Ethnobotanical surveys from different Moroccan regions show that remedies for “sugar disease” are frequently framed as cleansing, cooling, or strengthening agents, and some species are specifically mentioned for associated manifestations such as skin lesions, infections, or weakness rather than for blood sugar alone ref [99], ref [92], ref [100]. This symptom-oriented logic is consistent with broader North African and Mediterranean herbal practice, where treatment is directed at both the perceived cause and its visible consequences.

Use in relation to complications is especially evident in plants with overlapping reputations for antidiabetic, renal, vascular, digestive, or dermatological effects. Reviews of Moroccan medicinal plants repeatedly note that species employed for diabetes are also used for hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity, gastrointestinal discomfort, and wound care, suggesting that local therapeutic choices implicitly target cardiometabolic and microvascular risk constellations rather than isolated hyperglycaemia ref [101], ref [28]. Experimental literature on widely used taxa such as Trigonella foenum-graecum and Olea europaea further supports this overlap, as these plants have documented hypoglycaemic, hypolipidaemic, antioxidant, and tissue-protective properties relevant to diabetic complications ref [102], ref [103].

At the same time, the complication-focused use of medicinal plants also raises safety questions, because patients may combine multiple remedies over long periods in response to chronic symptoms such as neuropathic pain, edema, or recurrent infections. Reviews of herbal medicines in diabetes emphasize that while antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions may be beneficial, prolonged unsupervised use can create variability in dosing, herb-drug interactions, and nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic risk—issues of particular importance in people already vulnerable to diabetic kidney or liver dysfunction ref [104].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Therapeutic Practices and Modes of Use
subsections.content:
In Moroccan ethnomedical practice, the boundary between food and remedy is often deliberately porous. Many plants used in diabetes self-care are everyday culinary materials—seeds, leaves, spices, condiments, and herbal infusions—consumed as part of meals or as habitual beverages rather than as sharply separated “medicines.” Ethnobotanical surveys from different Moroccan regions repeatedly note the prominence of edible or condiment species such as fenugreek, cinnamon, olive, garlic, onion, and aromatic Lamiaceae taxa in antidiabetic repertoires, illustrating how glycemic control is embedded within ordinary domestic consumption patterns as much as within formal therapeutic acts ref [72], ref [105], ref [92].

This continuum has practical and cultural implications. First, routinized ingestion through soups, breads, teas, and spice mixtures supports chronic use for a long-term condition such as diabetes, while minimizing the social stigma associated with drug-taking. Second, the food frame permits dose flexibility: the same plant may be taken as a stronger decoction when symptoms worsen, or in smaller dietary amounts for maintenance. Such uses align with broader Mediterranean and North African traditions in which olive products, culinary herbs, and bitter or aromatic plants are valued simultaneously for nourishment, digestion, and metabolic balance ref [106], ref [107].

From a pharmacological perspective, this food-medicine overlap is plausible because several commonly consumed Moroccan taxa have documented hypoglycemic or insulin-sensitizing potential, including Trigonella foenum-graecum, Cinnamomum species, Olea europaea, and Allium species ref [108], ref [109], ref [110]. Nonetheless, the apparent safety conferred by “food” status can obscure risks linked to concentrated preparations, cumulative intake, or concomitant use with antidiabetic drugs. For survey interpretation, the Moroccan case therefore underscores that antidiabetic plant use cannot be understood solely through a medicinal lens; it also operates through dietary habit, seasonality, household economy, and culturally normalized preventive eating.

subsections.section_title: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evidence Supporting Antidiabetic Use
subsections.content:
The Moroccan medicinal flora used against diabetes is chemically dominated by a few recurrent phytochemical classes, especially polyphenols, terpenoids, alkaloids, sulfur compounds, and saponins. Phenolic acids, flavonoids, tannins, and related oligomers are particularly prominent because they are abundant in many Lamiaceae, Asteraceae, Oleaceae, and Myrtaceae species and are consistently associated with glucose-lowering, antioxidant, and enzyme-inhibitory effects ref [111], ref [112]. Reviews of antidiabetic phytochemicals further indicate that flavonoids such as quercetin derivatives, catechins, luteolin, apigenin, and rutin, together with phenolic acids such as chlorogenic, caffeic, and rosmarinic acids, are among the most widely implicated molecules in plant-based glycemic control ref [113], ref [114].

Terpenoid constituents form a second major group. Monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes concentrated in aromatic Moroccan taxa may contribute to antihyperglycemic activity through digestive enzyme modulation and improvement of insulin sensitivity, while triterpenes and sterols such as oleanolic acid, ursolic acid, and β-sitosterol have been broadly linked to metabolic benefits ref [115], ref [116]. In parallel, alkaloids remain pharmacologically important despite their lower taxonomic distribution, as classic examples such as berberine illustrate the capacity of this class to influence hepatic glucose production, insulin signaling, and gut-mediated effects ref [117].

Other classes also deserve attention when interpreting traditional Moroccan remedies. Organosulfur compounds, especially those characteristic of Allium species, have long been associated with hypoglycemic activity, whereas steroidal or triterpenoid saponins may slow carbohydrate absorption and improve insulin action ref [118], ref [113]. Overall, the antidiabetic potential of Moroccan plants is therefore best understood as a chemically plural phenomenon in which polyphenol-rich extracts are common, but terpenoids, alkaloids, sulfur compounds, and saponins may substantially shape bioactivity depending on species identity, extraction method, and phytochemical synergy.

subsections.section_title: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evidence Supporting Antidiabetic Use
subsections.content:
The antihyperglycemic effects reported for Moroccan medicinal plants can be interpreted through a limited set of recurrent mechanisms. A first major route is attenuation of postprandial glucose excursions by inhibiting intestinal carbohydrate digestion and absorption. This includes suppression of α-glucosidase and α-amylase activity, an approach validated clinically by acarbose and discussed extensively for plant polyphenols, flavonoids, and tannins ref [119], ref [120]. In parallel, some phytochemicals may reduce intestinal glucose transport and thereby blunt glucose entry into the circulation ref [121].

A second mechanism involves improved peripheral glucose disposal and hepatic metabolic control. Many plant-derived phenolics and terpenoids activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), enhance insulin signaling, or promote GLUT4 translocation, thereby increasing skeletal-muscle glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis ref [122], ref [123]. Related effects on peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ) and adipocyte differentiation may further improve insulin sensitivity, although this can vary by compound class ref [124].

A third, complementary mechanism is protection of pancreatic β-cells and mitigation of glucolipotoxicity-driven inflammation and oxidative stress. Chronic hyperglycemia is tightly linked to reactive oxygen species generation and inflammatory signaling that impair insulin secretion and insulin action ref [125]. Accordingly, phytochemicals with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties may preserve β-cell function, improve insulin secretory responses, and secondarily normalize glycemia ref [125], ref [126]. Taken together, the antihyperglycemic actions attributed to traditional Moroccan remedies are plausibly multitarget, combining intestinal, pancreatic, hepatic, and peripheral effects.

subsections.section_title: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evidence Supporting Antidiabetic Use
subsections.content:
Oxidative stress and low-grade inflammation are central to the progression of insulin resistance and diabetic complications, so the antioxidant profile of Moroccan medicinal plants is pharmacologically relevant rather than merely ancillary. Polyphenol-rich extracts commonly used in Moroccan ethnomedicine—especially those containing flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, and terpenoids—can attenuate lipid peroxidation, preserve endogenous antioxidant defenses, and limit redox-sensitive inflammatory signaling. More broadly, hyperglycemia-driven overproduction of reactive oxygen species promotes activation of NF-κB, cytokine release, and endothelial dysfunction, thereby linking antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects to glycemic control and tissue protection ref [125], ref [127].

This rationale is consistent with studies on species frequently cited in North African and Mediterranean traditional medicine. Olive leaf phenolics, notably oleuropein and hydroxytyrosol derivatives, show strong radical-scavenging and anti-inflammatory properties and have been associated with improved metabolic homeostasis ref [128]. Argan oil and its minor phenolic and tocopherol fractions also display antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions that may help explain reported benefits on metabolic risk markers ref [129]. Likewise, rosemary diterpenes such as carnosic acid and carnosol are well documented as inhibitors of oxidative and inflammatory pathways ref [130], while thyme species rich in thymol and carvacrol exhibit complementary antioxidant and immunomodulatory effects ref [131].

At the mechanistic level, these botanicals may reduce diabetes-related damage by enhancing superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione systems, while suppressing TNF-α, IL-6, COX-2, and iNOS expression through modulation of NF-κB and related pathways ref [127], ref [130], ref [132]. Such actions are particularly relevant because antioxidant and anti-inflammatory interventions can mitigate β-cell vulnerability and improve insulin signaling even when direct hypoglycemic effects are modest ref [125], ref [133]. Accordingly, the redox- and inflammation-modulating properties of Moroccan medicinal plants should be regarded as an integral component of their antidiabetic potential.

subsections.section_title: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evidence Supporting Antidiabetic Use
subsections.content:
In vitro studies provide an important first layer of support for the antidiabetic use of Moroccan medicinal plants by identifying direct effects on carbohydrate digestion, glucose handling, and insulin-related pathways. A recurrent finding is inhibition of digestive enzymes, particularly α-amylase and α-glucosidase, by phenolic-rich extracts. Such activity has been reported for edible and medicinal species widely used in North Africa, including argan by-products and pomegranate peel, whose polyphenol-enriched fractions strongly suppress these enzymes in cell-free assays, thereby supporting a mechanistic basis for attenuation of postprandial hyperglycemia ref [134], ref [135]. Similar observations have been made more broadly for culinary and medicinal plants of the Mediterranean pharmacopoeia, where flavonoids, tannins, and phenolic acids emerge as major contributors to enzyme inhibition ref [136].

Beyond enzyme assays, cell-based models indicate that several plant phenolics relevant to Moroccan materia medica can modulate glucose uptake and insulin signaling. Rosmarinic-acid-rich preparations from Lamiaceae plants, for example, have been shown to enhance glucose consumption in insulin-responsive cells and to influence AMP-activated protein kinase and related metabolic targets ref [137]. Cinnamaldehyde and cinnamon polyphenols, frequently used as comparative benchmarks in antidiabetic phytotherapy research, also improve insulin receptor signaling and glucose uptake in adipocyte models ref [138]. Likewise, olive-leaf secoiridoids such as oleuropein and hydroxytyrosol have demonstrated protective effects against glucotoxicity and favorable modulation of glucose transport and oxidative stress in cultured cells ref [139].

Collectively, these in vitro data support several plausible mechanisms for traditionally used Moroccan plants: delayed intestinal carbohydrate hydrolysis, improved peripheral glucose utilization, and reduction of oxidative damage that contributes to β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous because extraction procedures, phytochemical standardization, and assay conditions vary markedly across studies. Accordingly, in vitro findings are best interpreted as mechanistic indicators that require confirmation in animal models and, ultimately, clinical studies ref [136], ref [140], ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evidence Supporting Antidiabetic Use
subsections.subsection_title: Evidence from in vivo experimental models
subsections.content:
In vivo evidence provides an important bridge between ethnomedicinal claims and mechanistic pharmacology. For several Moroccan medicinal plants, antihyperglycemic activity has been demonstrated in alloxan- or streptozotocin-induced diabetic rodents as well as in normoglycemic glucose-loading models. Aqueous or hydroethanolic preparations of Nigella sativa seeds lowered blood glucose and improved lipid abnormalities in diabetic rats, findings that support earlier observations of a genuine antidiabetic effect beyond acute insulin release ref [142]. Likewise, Trigonella foenum-graecum seed preparations repeatedly reduced hyperglycemia and improved oral glucose tolerance in experimental diabetes, consistent with actions on carbohydrate absorption and peripheral glucose utilization ref [143].

Among plants commonly used in North Africa, Artemisia herba-alba has shown clear hypoglycemic activity in diabetic rodents, including reductions in fasting glycemia after repeated administration ref [144]. Olea europaea leaf extracts also produced antihyperglycemic effects in alloxan-diabetic rats and were accompanied in some studies by improved oxidative status, suggesting that glycemic benefit may be linked to both insulin-sensitizing and antioxidant mechanisms ref [145]. Similar in vivo support exists for Origanum compactum and Globularia alypum, whose extracts decreased blood glucose in experimental models and thereby lend pharmacological credibility to their traditional use in Moroccan folk medicine ref [5,6].

However, this body of evidence remains methodologically uneven. Doses, extraction procedures, duration of treatment, and diabetic models vary widely, and many studies rely on crude extracts without standardization of active constituents. Even so, the convergence of positive findings across multiple rodent models—together with occasional improvements in body weight, serum lipids, and markers of oxidative stress—indicates that at least a subset of Moroccan antidiabetic plants merits further preclinical development under more rigorous experimental designs ref [3,7,8].

subsections.section_title: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evidence Supporting Antidiabetic Use
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative appraisal of traditional claims and experimental findings
subsections.content:
A comparative reading of ethnobotanical records and pharmacological studies suggests that many Moroccan antidiabetic claims are directionally supported, but the strength of evidence remains uneven. Plants frequently cited in traditional practice, such as Trigonella foenum-graecum, Nigella sativa and Artemisia herba-alba, also show glucose-lowering, insulin-sensitizing or enzyme-inhibitory effects in experimental systems, lending biological plausibility to their continued use ref [150], ref [151], ref [152]. Likewise, globally recognized antidiabetic botanicals with relevance to North African materia medica, including Olea europaea and Allium sativum, display hypoglycemic and antioxidant activities consistent with folk indications ref [153], ref [154].

However, concordance between traditional reputation and experimental validation is often only partial. Most positive findings derive from in vitro assays or rodent models using standardized extracts at doses that do not necessarily reflect customary preparations, while phytochemical composition can vary substantially with geography, harvest season and extraction method ref [152], ref [153], ref [155]. Moreover, many studies focus on acute glycemic endpoints or surrogate markers rather than long-term metabolic control, and rigorous clinical confirmation remains scarce even for widely used species ref [150], ref [156].

Overall, the available evidence supports the view that traditional Moroccan knowledge has been a productive guide for identifying antidiabetic plants, but it should not be interpreted as equivalent to clinical proof. Future work should prioritize species with both high ethnobotanical consensus and reproducible preclinical efficacy, while integrating authentication, standardization, toxicity assessment and controlled human studies to distinguish genuinely effective remedies from culturally salient but insufficiently validated ones ref [155], ref [156], ref [157].

subsections.section_title: Safety, Toxicological Considerations, and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Although many antidiabetic botanicals are perceived as intrinsically safe, adverse effects remain a major translational concern because toxicity depends on plant species, extraction method, dose, duration, and host vulnerability. A broad review of herbal medicines has emphasized that hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and contamination-related harms are recurrent patterns rather than exceptional events ref [158]. In diabetes, these risks are amplified by common comorbid renal and hepatic impairment, which can alter the disposition of phytochemicals and increase susceptibility to organ injury.

Liver injury is one of the best documented serious adverse outcomes. A systematic review of herb-induced liver injury identified numerous implicated medicinal plants and highlighted diagnostic difficulties arising from multi-ingredient preparations and variable product quality ref [159]. Experimental work also shows that some antidiabetic plants have narrow safety margins at higher doses; for example, subchronic administration of Artemisia afra extract produced organ toxicity in rats, despite the ethnopharmacological popularity of the genus ref [160]. Such findings caution against extrapolating efficacy studies directly into chronic human use.

Even widely used species can produce clinically relevant toxicity. Cases of hypoglycemia, gastrointestinal intolerance, allergic reactions, and reproductive toxicity have been reported with commonly consumed herbal products, while plant-specific concerns include cinnamon-associated coumarin hepatotoxicity ref [161] and hepatotoxicity signals linked to Aloe vera preparations ref [162]. Fenugreek has shown developmental toxicity in experimental models, underscoring concerns for pregnancy exposure ref [163]. More broadly, the WHO has stressed that adverse events from herbal medicines are often underreported and complicated by misidentification, adulteration, and contamination with heavy metals or undeclared pharmaceuticals ref [164].

subsections.section_title: Safety, Toxicological Considerations, and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Herb–drug interactions are a particular concern in diabetes because many patients combine medicinal plants with metformin, sulfonylureas, insulin, statins, antihypertensives, and antiplatelet agents. The main risks are pharmacodynamic additivity, leading to unintended hypoglycemia, and pharmacokinetic interactions mediated by drug-metabolizing enzymes or transporters. Systematic reviews of herb–drug interactions note that botanicals can alter cytochrome P450 activity, P-glycoprotein transport, and glucose handling, making polypharmacy in diabetes especially vulnerable to unpredictable responses ref [165], ref [166].

Several commonly used antidiabetic plants or supplements have plausible interaction liabilities. Cinnamon, fenugreek, bitter melon, ginseng, aloe vera, and Gymnema sylvestre have all been reported to lower glucose and may potentiate conventional agents when used concurrently ref [167], ref [168]. In parallel, well-studied botanicals such as St John’s wort can induce CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, reducing exposure to co-administered drugs, whereas ginkgo and garlic may increase bleeding risk when combined with aspirin or anticoagulants often prescribed to diabetic patients with cardiovascular disease ref [169], ref [170]. These interaction patterns are clinically relevant even when evidence is based on case reports, small trials, or mechanistic studies rather than definitive outcome trials.

Translation to practice is hindered by variable plant composition, underreporting of supplement use, and limited interaction testing in diabetic populations. Reviews focused on diabetes management emphasize the need for medication reconciliation, active surveillance for hypoglycemia, and caution when botanicals are introduced or discontinued around established drug regimens ref [168], ref [171], ref [172]. In clinical settings, the safest approach is to treat plant products as pharmacologically active co-medications rather than benign dietary adjuncts.

subsections.section_title: Safety, Toxicological Considerations, and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Dose standardization is a major barrier to translating antidiabetic medicinal plants into reproducible therapy. In contrast to single-molecule drugs, botanical preparations vary according to species identity, genotype, plant part, harvest season, geography, post-harvest processing, and extraction solvent, all of which can substantially alter concentrations of putatively active constituents and therefore biological potency ref [173], ref [174]. This problem is especially relevant in diabetes, where modest differences in glycemic activity may shift a preparation from inefficacy to clinically meaningful glucose lowering or, conversely, to hypoglycemia when combined with standard drugs.

A further challenge is that many antidiabetic plants contain multiple compound classes acting on different targets, making it difficult to define the appropriate basis for dosing. Standardization to a single marker compound may improve manufacturing consistency yet fail to reflect the true bioactive profile, while absence of validated pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic markers limits rational dose selection and comparison across studies ref [175], ref [176]. Even for comparatively well-studied botanicals, analytical and clinical reviews have emphasized batch-to-batch variability and inconsistent reporting of extract ratio, marker content, and daily dose, undermining meta-analysis and evidence synthesis ref [177], ref [178].

Addressing these issues requires a shift from crude weight-based dosing toward chemically and biologically characterized preparations. WHO guidance and broader herbal standardization literature recommend authenticated raw materials, specification of extraction procedures, quantification of relevant markers, stability testing, and linkage of phytochemical fingerprints to pharmacological activity ref [174], ref [179], ref [180]. For diabetes-focused products, such frameworks are essential if preclinical efficacy is to be translated into reliable, safe, and comparable clinical dosing regimens.

subsections.section_title: Safety, Toxicological Considerations, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Quality control and authentication of medicinal plant materials
subsections.content:
Quality control is a central translational bottleneck for antidiabetic medicinal plants because efficacy and safety depend on correct species identity, plant part, harvest stage, processing, and storage. Substitution, adulteration, and geographic chemotypic variation can markedly alter phytochemical profiles, making literature on one preparation difficult to generalize to another. The World Health Organization has therefore emphasized pharmacognostic standardization, contaminant testing, and traceable sourcing as minimum requirements for herbal medicines ref [181]. Broader analyses of herbal quality failures similarly identify misidentification and inconsistent composition as recurrent causes of unreliable biological and clinical findings ref [182].

Authentication should ideally combine classical botany with chemical and molecular tools. Macroscopic and microscopic examination remain useful for raw materials, but chromatographic fingerprinting provides batch-level assessment of marker compounds and overall compositional consistency; HPLC- and TLC-based approaches have been widely advocated for complex botanicals ref [183], ref [184]. DNA barcoding can strengthen species-level authentication, especially for fragmented or powdered materials where morphology is lost, although it should complement rather than replace phytochemical testing because it does not capture active-metabolite abundance or post-harvest degradation ref [185], ref [186].

For plants used in diabetes, quality systems must also address contaminants with direct metabolic relevance, including pesticides, heavy metals, aflatoxins, and undeclared synthetic antidiabetic drugs sometimes found in commercial herbal products. Validated good agricultural and collection practices and good manufacturing practices are therefore necessary to support reproducibility, pharmacovigilance, and eventual regulatory approval ref [181], ref [179], ref [187]. In practice, clinically credible development requires voucher specimens, authenticated supply chains, predefined chemical specifications, and stability data linking the tested material to the marketed product.

subsections.section_title: Safety, Toxicological Considerations, and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Clinical evidence supporting antidiabetic medicinal plants remains uneven. Although several randomized or controlled studies report modest improvements in glycemic indices for selected botanicals such as cinnamon, aloe vera, and berberine-containing preparations, results are often inconsistent across trials and meta-analyses because of small sample sizes, short follow-up, heterogeneous endpoints, and poorly characterized interventions ref [188], ref [189], ref [190]. Even when benefits are observed, they are frequently comparable to adjunctive rather than stand-alone effects, limiting direct translation into routine diabetes care ref [190], ref [191].

A major translational gap is the mismatch between preclinical promise and clinical reproducibility. Animal and in vitro studies commonly use standardized extracts, defined doses, and controlled disease models, whereas human studies often evaluate crude powders or commercial mixtures with variable phytochemical composition. This problem is well illustrated in cinnamon trials, where species differences, coumarin content, and formulation variability complicate interpretation of efficacy and safety ref [188], ref [192]. Similar concerns apply broadly to herbal medicines, for which CONSORT-style reporting of botanical identity, extraction methods, marker compounds, and batch consistency is still incomplete ref [193].

Clinical translation is further constrained by limited long-term safety data, inadequate assessment of herb-drug interactions in patients already receiving metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin, and sparse evidence for hard outcomes such as complications or cardiovascular risk ref [191], ref [194]. Future studies need rigorously authenticated materials, pharmacokinetic characterization, dose-finding designs, and multicenter trials aligned with modern standards for diabetes therapeutics before plant-based interventions can move from complementary use toward evidence-based integration ref [193], ref [195].

subsections.section_title: Safety, Toxicological Considerations, and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Regulatory oversight of plant-derived antidiabetic products remains heterogeneous across jurisdictions, creating major translational uncertainty. In many settings, herbal medicines are marketed as foods, supplements, or traditional remedies rather than as drugs, which lowers premarket evidentiary requirements for efficacy and shifts emphasis toward postmarketing surveillance. The World Health Organization has repeatedly argued that national policies should integrate quality, safety, efficacy assessment, pharmacovigilance, and practitioner regulation for traditional medicines, but implementation remains uneven ref [196]. This is especially problematic in diabetes, where long-term use, polypharmacy, and narrow therapeutic targets increase the consequences of under-regulated products.

Ethically, clinical use and research on medicinal plants for diabetes must address informed consent, realistic communication of benefit, and protection against substitution of unvalidated remedies for evidence-based care. Reporting standards for herbal interventions were developed precisely because inadequate characterization of plant material, extraction, and dosing undermines reproducibility and participant protection ref [197], ref [198]. International ethical guidance also emphasizes scientific validity, favorable risk-benefit balance, and responsiveness to local health needs in human studies ref [199]. For traditional knowledge-based products, additional ethical issues concern fair attribution, prior informed consent, and equitable benefit-sharing with Indigenous and local communities, as formalized in the Nagoya Protocol ref [200].

A further regulatory challenge is the boundary between botanical drugs and traditional herbal products. The U.S. FDA’s botanical drug framework illustrates a pathway for complex plant mixtures, but still requires robust chemistry, manufacturing control, and clinical evidence comparable to other therapeutics ref [201]. Experience with approved botanical drugs shows that standardization and regulatory acceptance are possible, yet difficult for multi-component preparations ref [202]. For antidiabetic plants, ethically responsible translation therefore requires stronger trial registration, adverse-event reporting, traceable sourcing, and compliance with good agricultural and collection practices to reduce both patient risk and exploitation of biodiversity ref [196], ref [179].

subsections.section_title: Conservation, Knowledge Preservation, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Sustainability of harvesting practices is a central concern for medicinal plants used in Moroccan diabetes care because demand can intensify pressure on wild populations, especially where roots, bark, bulbs, or whole plants are collected. Ethnobotanical surveys from Morocco repeatedly show that many antidiabetic remedies rely on species harvested from natural habitats and that destructive collection remains common for some taxa, increasing the risk of local depletion when commercialization expands ref [72], ref [92]. More broadly, Mediterranean and North African medicinal floras are exposed to the combined effects of overharvesting, grazing pressure, drought, and land-use change, making harvesting method an important determinant of long-term availability ref [203], ref [204].

A sustainable strategy should therefore prioritize non-destructive collection protocols: preferential use of leaves, flowers, or fruits where pharmacologically acceptable; seasonal harvesting after seed set; rotational collection sites; and explicit limits on the proportion of biomass removed from each population. For high-value wild species, cultivation and domestication are especially important, as argued in global assessments of medicinal plant conservation and trade ref [205], ref [206]. Good Agricultural and Collection Practices provide a practical framework for Morocco by linking species identification, habitat monitoring, traceability, and post-harvest quality control to both conservation and pharmacological reproducibility ref [179].

Future Moroccan research should move beyond listing useful plants to quantifying harvest pressure, regeneration rates, and market chains for the most frequently used antidiabetic species. Community-based resource management, participatory mapping of collection areas, and incentives for local cultivation would help align livelihood needs with biodiversity stewardship. Such approaches are consistent with evidence that medicinal plant conservation is most effective when ecological monitoring, local knowledge, and value-chain governance are addressed together ref [204], ref [206], ref [207].

subsections.section_title: Conservation, Knowledge Preservation, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Conservation of endemic and threatened taxa
subsections.content:
Conservation of endemic and threatened medicinal taxa in Morocco is a central prerequisite for the long-term viability of traditional diabetes care. Morocco forms part of the Mediterranean biodiversity hotspot, where high endemism coincides with intense anthropogenic pressure, including overharvesting, overgrazing, land-use change, and climatic stressors ref [208], ref [209]. These pressures are especially consequential for slow-growing aromatic and medicinal species collected from the wild, because repeated extraction of reproductive or subterranean organs can rapidly erode local population viability.

Evidence from North Africa and the Mediterranean indicates that medicinal species with narrow ecological ranges or high commercial demand are particularly vulnerable when harvesting is unmanaged. In Morocco, this concern is salient for taxa in genera such as Thymus, Origanum, Artemisia, and endemic Lamiaceae and Asteraceae assemblages associated with mountain and arid ecosystems. Conservation planning should therefore prioritize in situ protection of high-endemism habitats, population-level monitoring, and the incorporation of IUCN Red List criteria into national assessments of medicinal plants ref [210], ref [211]. Ex situ measures, including seed banking and living collections, can complement field conservation, particularly for species whose habitats are fragmented or whose regeneration is weak ref [212].

A pragmatic approach is to couple ethnobotanical value with conservation status when setting priorities: species that are both culturally important and biologically restricted deserve urgent management attention. Such prioritization is consistent with broader Mediterranean conservation frameworks and with guidance on preserving crop wild relatives and useful wild plants under accelerating environmental change ref [213], ref [214]. For Moroccan ethnopharmacology, conservation should thus be treated not as a parallel agenda, but as a foundational condition for future pharmacological validation, equitable bioprospecting, and continuity of local therapeutic traditions.

subsections.section_title: Conservation, Knowledge Preservation, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Preservation of indigenous and local knowledge
subsections.content:
Preserving indigenous and local knowledge is central to the future of Moroccan medicinal-plant use because therapeutic practices are embedded in orally transmitted vocabularies, harvesting rules, preparation techniques, and culturally specific disease concepts. Ethnobotanical work in Morocco has repeatedly shown that this knowledge remains unevenly distributed across age, gender, occupation, and locality, with increasing risks of erosion under urbanization, migration, and changing health-seeking behavior ref [215], ref [216]. Similar concerns have been documented globally, where rapid loss of biocultural knowledge accompanies social and ecological change ref [217], ref [218].

In practical terms, preservation requires more than compiling plant lists. High-quality documentation should record vernacular nomenclature, plant-part selection, dosage, contraindications, market pathways, and the social contexts in which remedies are validated and transmitted. Standardized quantitative ethnobotanical methods can improve comparability and reduce the loss of fine-grained information that often disappears when knowledge holders are no longer available ref [219], ref [220]. For Morocco, priority should be given to multilingual, community-linked archives that capture Arabic, Amazigh, and region-specific terminologies alongside voucher specimens and georeferenced ecological data.

Knowledge preservation must also be ethically grounded. International norms emphasize prior informed consent, community participation, and fair treatment of holders of traditional knowledge, especially when documentation may feed into commercialization or biomedical research ref [221]. The Convention on Biological Diversity and the Nagoya Protocol provide an important policy framework for linking conservation, access, and benefit-sharing ref [222]. Accordingly, Moroccan research agendas should move toward co-produced documentation, local educational transmission, and community-controlled repositories so that safeguarding knowledge supports both cultural continuity and equitable innovation.

subsections.section_title: Conservation, Knowledge Preservation, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Integration of ethnobotany with modern drug discovery
subsections.content:
Integrating Moroccan ethnobotany with modern drug discovery requires treating traditional use not as proof of efficacy, but as a rational prioritization tool. Ethnopharmacological selection can enrich screening libraries for antidiabetic leads, especially when combined with phylogenetic information, chemotaxonomy, and transparent recording of preparation modes and dose forms ref [223], ref [224]. For diabetes-related indications, such prioritization should move beyond crude “hypoglycemic” claims toward mechanism-linked workflows that test effects on intestinal carbohydrate digestion, insulin signaling, hepatic glucose output, oxidative stress, inflammation, and protection from glucolipotoxicity.

A productive pipeline is therefore iterative: voucher-based field documentation, extract standardization, bioassay-guided fractionation, dereplication by LC-MS/NMR, and early ADME-toxicity assessment. This approach has been strengthened by broader natural-products drug-discovery frameworks emphasizing prefractionation, metabolomics, and avoidance of rediscovering known compounds ref [225], ref [226]. It is also important to recognize the limits of single-target screening; many plant preparations act through polypharmacology and synergy, themes increasingly addressed through network pharmacology and systems-level analysis ref [227].

For Morocco, the most valuable near-term strategy is to connect high-consensus medicinal taxa with reproducible phytochemical fingerprints and clinically relevant models, then advance only the best-characterized candidates into well-designed translational studies. Such integration should be accompanied by ethical benefit-sharing and protection of community intellectual contributions, in line with international principles on access and equitable use of biodiversity-derived resources ref [228], ref [200]. If rigorously implemented, ethnobotanical knowledge can thus serve as a discovery compass for safer, culturally grounded antidiabetic interventions rather than remaining an isolated descriptive archive.

subsections.section_title: Conservation, Knowledge Preservation, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Methodological priorities for Moroccan medicinal-plant research should begin with greater rigor and reproducibility in ethnobotanical documentation. Sampling strategies, voucher deposition, transparent taxonomic verification, and quantitative indices should be standardized to reduce the well-known problems of inconsistent reporting and limited comparability across studies ref [219], ref [229]. In parallel, studies on antidiabetic plants should better distinguish food, herbal, and polyherbal uses, record preparation dose and duration, and incorporate sociolinguistic context so that therapeutic claims are interpretable rather than merely enumerative.

A second priority is to move beyond descriptive inventories toward hypothesis-driven pharmacology. Reviews of ethnopharmacological practice have emphasized the need for selection criteria grounded in traditional use, bioassay relevance, and phytochemical plausibility ref [230]. For diabetes-oriented research, this implies using mechanistically coherent assays—such as glucose uptake, insulin secretion, intestinal enzyme inhibition, and inflammation/oxidative-stress endpoints—rather than relying only on single in vitro tests. Extract standardization, metabolomic profiling, and authentication tools such as DNA barcoding can improve traceability and comparability of plant materials ref [185], ref [231].

Finally, translational credibility requires stronger attention to safety, biostatistics, and reporting quality. Many medicinal plants can produce herb-induced liver injury or clinically relevant herb-drug interactions, issues that are especially important in patients already receiving antidiabetic therapy ref [232], ref [233]. Future Moroccan studies should therefore integrate toxicology, pharmacokinetics, preregistered protocols, and adherence to CONSORT guidance for herbal interventions in randomized trials ref [234]. Such methodological upgrades would make local knowledge more actionable for evidence-based diabetes care and conservation policy.

subsections.section_title: Conservation, Knowledge Preservation, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Toward integrative diabetes care in Morocco
subsections.content:
Toward integrative diabetes care in Morocco, medicinal plants should be positioned as complementary rather than substitutive therapies within patient-centred chronic disease management. This requires acknowledging the widespread use of traditional remedies while aligning practice with evidence-based diabetes standards, including structured diagnosis, glycaemic monitoring, cardiovascular risk reduction, and screening for renal, retinal, and neuropathic complications as emphasized in international clinical guidance ref [235], ref [236]. Because many Moroccan herbal preparations are used alongside conventional drugs, the central policy challenge is not simply efficacy testing, but safe co-management, dose standardization, and recognition of herb–drug interactions in routine care.

An integrative model should therefore combine ethnobotanical knowledge with rigorous translational evaluation. The WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy argues for regulated incorporation of traditional medicine into national health systems, with attention to quality, safety, and practitioner training ref [196]. In diabetes specifically, consensus reports stress individualized lifestyle and pharmacologic care and the importance of culturally appropriate self-management support ref [237]. For Moroccan contexts, this implies documenting plant use patterns in primary care, identifying botanicals with plausible antihyperglycaemic or complication-modifying effects, and prioritizing toxicological assessment of the preparations most frequently consumed.

Implementation will depend on pragmatic research and health-system design. Randomized and observational studies should evaluate standardized extracts as adjuncts to usual care, using outcomes relevant to long-term diabetes control rather than isolated in vitro endpoints. At the same time, implementation science can guide community-linked models that improve self-management and chronic care delivery in low- and middle-income settings ref [238], while broader analyses of diabetes burden in North Africa underscore the urgency of scalable prevention and treatment strategies ref [239]. In this framework, Moroccan integrative diabetes care should unite clinicians, pharmacists, ethnobotanists, and traditional knowledge holders within regulated referral, pharmacovigilance, and patient-education pathways.
